summary:
Junín department has no department-level statute, enforcement finding or incident series in the sourced material. The department stands under Peru's national framework, so what a trans visitor to Junín encounters is set in Lima: Peru does not criminalise trans identity or consensual same-sex activity, but the national legislature has legislated directly against trans people's use of public facilities, the Penal Code carries no hate-crime or discrimination protection on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and recorded violence against trans women is rising.

The restriction on restrooms was adopted in stages. On 20 February 2025 the congressional Women and Family Commission approved without dissent a dictamen merging bills 6506 and 8457, tabled by Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Muñante, barring trans people from restrooms that do not correspond to their birth sex. On 2 April 2025 the Plenary approved the bill and exempted it from a second vote; its article 5 forbids any person from entering or using a public sanitary service that does not correspond to their 'biological sex'. Law 32331, enacted 13 May 2025, carries the ban into force nationally and also prohibits inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'.

The exceptions are narrow: custody situations, cases requiring medical attention, and accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities. The stated trigger for the bills was a July 2023 social-media complaint about gendered restroom labels at Lima's Jorge Chávez airport. The April 2025 Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents extends the logic, mandating that public-restroom entry be determined by 'biological sex' and thereby barring trans youth as well as adults from facilities matching their identity; Human Rights Watch reports that its vaguely worded child-protection provisions, notably Article 4 on media and advertising and Article 5, enable censorship of identity-related, artistic and educational content, and that the minimum sentence for obscenity rose from three to four years.

LGTBIQ activist Gianna Camacho, co-author of a July 2024 report on rising hate crimes, calls the restroom measure discriminatory and warns that access would come to depend on security staff's personal judgment, including identity-document checks. She notes there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms. The IDEHPUCP human-rights institute of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, in an analysis by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte of 15 April 2025, holds that article 5 violates the equal-treatment and non-discrimination principle of article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights, and that the stated aim of preventing child sexual abuse rests on a stigmatising stereotype casting trans people as likely restroom harassers, while UN reporting shows trans people are more often victims than aggressors.

Recorded anti-LGBTI violence is high and, per the report's co-author, understated: national figures for 2020-2023 count 54 murders of TLGBI people and 170 rights-violation cases, with trans women more than half the homicide victims at 30, against 23 gay men and one lesbian. Killings rose to 19 in 2023, 12 of them trans women, from 13 in 2022, 10 in 2021 and 12 in 2020, many carried out with cruelty. The 170 cases include state violence and incitement to discrimination, with 61 complaints recorded in 2020. In February 2023 the trans sex worker Rubí Torres Silvano, 31, was abducted by a gang in central Lima and killed in Carabayllo with about 30 gunshots as part of an extortion scheme.

The torture and rape of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, ended in conviction on 15 December 2025: police officers Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León received 17 years' imprisonment, Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history. A 2012 Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia study found that 70% of trans women in Lima and Callao work in sex work, a documented exposure factor for police and public violence.
tangentialFactors:
Peru is one of only three South American countries, alongside Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in law. The removal of the protections followed a congressional vote of 66–29 in May 2017 to strip Decree Nº 1323, which had criminalised such discrimination from 7 January 2017 through Articles 46 and 323 of the Penal Code, and President Kuczynski's veto could not hold as the Penal Code was reworked. The repeal was carried by Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members arguing the President lacked authority to issue the decree.

The IDEHPUCP analysis and the institute's earlier work both invoke Inter-American Court of Human Rights Advisory Opinion OC-24/17, under which gender identity falls within protected personal autonomy and states must guarantee trans people's full rights, so the restroom regime sits in direct tension with binding regional standards. The institute also records dehumanising comparisons made by congressman Lizarzaburu on the plenary floor.

Official hostility is documented alongside the violence figures: Outright International reports that public institutions themselves contribute to anti-LGBTIQ discrimination, and in July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, struck an anti-equality decree as unconstitutional. An April 2025 law on foreign funding of NGOs lets authorities revoke registrations on 'public order and security' grounds, which risks being weaponised against queer organising. In April 2025 the television presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed the first openly-lesbian congresswoman, Susel Paredes, telling her to 'go use the men's room'.
localsOnly:
Trans Peruvians may change their legal name to match their gender identity. In 2014 the Constitutional Court barred gender-marker changes on national identity documents, then reversed itself in a ruling of 21 October 2016 published 8 November, permitting gender change through a judicial process without sex-reassignment surgery. A Gender Identity Law covering legal gender change without surgery and access to passports and other identity documents matching gender identity was introduced on 4 November 2016 and remained pending in the legislature as of March 2021.

Healthcare classifications shifted in both directions during 2024. In May the government decreed 'transsexualism' a mental health problem in order to cover trans healthcare; after protests, MINSA revised the term to 'gender discordance' in June 2024 for health-insurance classification purposes, and in the same month health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described by Human Rights Watch as a step toward dignity for trans patients.

Conversion therapy is banned in Peru for medical professionals, and in May 2024 MINSA reiterated that sexual orientation and gender identity are not diseases, a protection with direct bearing on trans and LGBTQ minors exposed to such practices.
outOfScopeNotes:
No sourced material addresses enforcement of Law 32331 or the April 2025 sexual-integrity law within Junín department: how security staff apply the restroom exceptions, whether identity-document checks occur in Huancayo or elsewhere in the department, and whether any local complaint has been filed are unresolved here.

The inventory does not state whether the congressional action of 2 April 2025 preceded or was consolidated into Law 32331 of 13 May 2025, and the relationship between the two instruments is presented as reported rather than as a settled legislative sequence.

Whether the pending Gender Identity Law has advanced since March 2021 is not sourced in this material. The resolution of the July 2023 complaint about restroom labelling at Jorge Chávez airport, beyond its role in prompting the bills, is also unsourced.

The 70% sex-work figure derives from a 2012 study limited to Lima and Callao and has no Junín-specific equivalent in the sources; no comparable local study is available here.
